items.title: “Eyeball to Eyeball”—Cuban Missile Crisis, Day Nine
items.summary: President John F. Kennedy’s hopes rise and then fall that the naval quarantine of Cuba will quickly end the missile crisis.

ai.sum: A CFR historical retrospective recounts President Kennedy's hopes and setbacks during the naval quarantine of Cuba in the missile crisis.

brief.summary: The authors, reviewing Day Nine of the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, describe President Kennedy's mounting pressure as the naval quarantine of Cuba took effect. They recount how moving the quarantine line from eight hundred to five hundred miles, on British advice, delayed the moment of decision about Soviet ships. They note that Soviet vessels had in fact turned back before the White House learned of it, so the feared confrontation at sea never occurred. Khrushchev's second letter then rejected the quarantine publicly, contrary to his private orders, and the authors conclude that the crisis's most dangerous days still lay ahead. The piece is a historical narrative built from ExComm records and the letters, and it offers no policy recommendations.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Kennedy's quarantine forced a dangerous decision point, but Khrushchev's contradictory second letter showed the crisis was far from over.

items.title: Dmytro Kuleba on Trump’s drift towards Moscow
items.summary: Dmytro Kuleba on Trump’s drift towards Moscow newspress_en Sat, 10/24/2026 - 06:00 Politics Nearly five years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Dmytro Kuleba sees no end in sight. Ukraine’s former foreign minister (2020-24), he steered Kyiv’s diplomacy for more than two years of the war, mainly during US President Joe Biden’s administration. Now a senior fellow at Harvard’s Belfer Centre, he believes the conflict is no longer just about territory, but about…

ai.sum: Former Ukrainian foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba analyses Trump's drift towards Moscow and sees no end to the war.

brief.summary: The authors, through former Ukrainian foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba, argue that the Russia-Ukraine war has shifted from a dispute over territory to a question of Putin's calculation that ending the war is riskier for him than continuing it. Kuleba holds that any ceasefire would quickly break down, that Ukraine's victory means preserved independence and a European orientation, and that sanctions constrain Russia without ending the war alone. He criticises US President Trump's drift towards Moscow and policies that restrain Ukraine's defensive capabilities, while rejecting the view that peace is imminent. He says NATO membership should stay on the table because no better security guarantee exists. On the Gulf, he expects limited engagement from Gulf capitals constrained by their ties to Moscow, calling Riyadh's drone-defence talks with Kyiv "a spike, not a strategy". He also defends Zelensky's blunt style as diplomacy that preserves room for dialogue.
brief.argument: Putin sees continuing the war as less risky than ending it, so Ukraine should prepare for a long confrontation and resist US policies that weaken it.
recommendations: Maintain support for Ukraine's defensive capabilities rather than restraining them
Keep NATO membership on the table as the best available security guarantee
Use sanctions as a constraint but not as a standalone route to ending the war
Expect limited durable Gulf engagement and treat Gulf offers as tactical rather than strategic

brief.summary: Türkiye's energy minister argues that energy security now means building resilient, diversified systems rather than simply securing supplies, amid geopolitical shocks, rising demand (including from AI) and climate goals. He contends energy security and decarbonisation should not be treated as competing aims but pursued through a balanced, pragmatic portfolio. He highlights renewables, efficiency, natural gas investment, a planned 20 GW of nuclear by 2050, critical minerals and regional interconnection as pillars. He presents the Saudi partnership, including a February 2026 agreement on up to 5,000 MW of solar and wind in Türkiye, as a model of regional cooperation, and frames connectivity as a basis for trust and interdependence.
brief.argument: Energy security in an uncertain world requires diversified, resilient systems and regional cooperation, pursued alongside rather than against the low-carbon transition.
recommendations: Pursue a balanced portfolio of renewables, nuclear, natural gas and efficiency rather than relying on any single source
Deepen regional electricity interconnection, storage and grid resilience
Modernise ageing energy infrastructure and invest in cleaner technologies
Secure diversified access to critical minerals through domestic development and external cooperation
brief.turkey: It sets out Türkiye's official energy doctrine, including the 2050 nuclear target, the Saudi renewables deal and the push to become a regional energy connectivity hub.

items.title: What’s at stake in Israel’s first elections since the October 7 attacks?
items.summary: An unclear outcome for Netanyahu or opponents could lead to prolonged coalition negotiations or even more elections. The post What’s at stake in Israel’s first elections since the October 7 attacks? appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis says Israel's first elections since October 7 could yield an unclear outcome, prolonging coalition talks or prompting further elections.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Israel's upcoming Knesset election may produce no clear governing path for either Netanyahu's bloc or its opponents, risking prolonged coalition talks or a repeat vote. They note polls show a deadlocked electorate, with the opposition likely needing Arab parties such as Ra'am to reach 61 seats, as in 2021. They frame the stakes around October 7 accountability, security posture, the Palestinian question, ultra-Orthodox military conscription and the cost of living. They describe Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu as likely to have little effect, given polls holding steady. They also outline the mechanics: a 3.25 percent threshold, the president's role in selecting a formateur, and unusual scenarios such as a minority government or an opposition-controlled Knesset speaker vote.
brief.argument: Israel's election is unlikely to produce a clear majority, so coalition arithmetic, especially the role of Arab parties, will decide who governs.

items.title: Here’s How Much Aid the United States Has Sent Ukraine
items.summary: Eleven charts illustrate the support the United States has provided Ukraine since Russia’s invasion—and how that support has changed since Trump took office.

ai.sum: CFR charts illustrate US military and financial aid to Ukraine since the invasion and how it changed under Trump.

brief.summary: The authors track how much aid the United States has sent Ukraine since Russia's February 2022 invasion, framing it through charts. They estimate $196 billion in Congress-approved spending tied to the war as of June 30, 2026, of which about $127 billion directly supports the Ukrainian government, and note that much of the money was spent on U.S. defence production. They argue U.S. commitment has shifted sharply under the second Trump administration, with no significant new aid legislation since April 2024 and the Patriot interceptor supply and intelligence sharing facing disruptions in October 2026. Using Kiel Institute data, they contend that European countries have collectively given more aid than the United States and have sharply increased support in 2025 and 2026, including a 90 billion euro EU loan. The piece also places U.S. aid against other recipients and against U.S. domestic spending for comparison.
brief.argument: U.S. aid to Ukraine was historically unprecedented in scale, but it has stalled under the second Trump administration while Europe has become the larger donor.

items.title: What will end Trump’s back-and-forth approach toward Russia and Ukraine
items.summary: Can pressure from Congress and the American public push Trump to take a tougher stance against Putin? The post What will end Trump’s back-and-forth approach toward Russia and Ukraine appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis asks whether Congress or public pressure could push Trump toward a tougher stance on Putin.

brief.summary: The authors argue that after Trump's October 9 diesel deal with Putin, his administration tilted toward Moscow: it pressed Ukraine to halt refinery strikes, pushed an energy ceasefire Russia ignored, reportedly disrupted US intelligence and Starlink/Starshield support to Kyiv, and waived sanctions under the 2026 Russia and Iran sanctions act. Bipartisan US criticism then put the administration on the defensive, and Witkoff's Oslo and Moscow trips led to a Kremlin readiness to resume trilateral talks in November, though not at summit level. The authors see the administration possibly changing course but treat its approach as erratic. They say the clearest signal to watch is whether Starlink and Starshield restrictions on Ukraine continue, and that Congress, especially in the lame-duck session, can push policy toward blunting Russian aggression.
brief.argument: Trump's Russia and Ukraine policy has swung back and forth, and only sustained external pressure, particularly from Congress, is likely to keep it aligned with US interests against Putin.
recommendations: Keep Starlink and Starshield support for Ukraine unrestricted as the key test of policy direction
Use the lame-duck session to insist on reversing the sanctions waiver and other concessions to Russia before advancing other White House legislation
Pursue congressional investigation of the administration's recent Russia policy decisions

items.title: Will the United States Attack Iran After the Midterms?
items.summary: After nearly nine months of war with Iran, President Donald Trump faces a choice: escalate the conflict with Tehran, find a way to coexist, or stand pat.

ai.sum: After nearly nine months of war with Iran, Trump faces a choice between escalating, coexisting or standing pat, per CFR analysis.

brief.summary: The authors (James Lindsay, interviewing Cole Bucy and Nate Swanson) examine whether Trump will escalate against Iran after the November 3 midterms, nearly nine months into a war. Lindsay frames Trump's options as escalate, negotiate, or stand pat, and argues each carries heavy downsides: renewed strikes may fail to topple the regime while Iran hits Gulf energy infrastructure, sanctioning China risks a financial shock and critical-minerals retaliation, and waiting gives Iran time to rebuild. Stalemate is strained by the naval blockade's costs to US forces and persistent energy prices. Bucy and Swanson's core test is whether Iran is an existential threat; if not, the authors suggest seeking a deal that stops attacks on shipping rather than paying to remove the regime.
brief.argument: Whether the US escalates against Iran after the midterms depends on whether Iran is an existential threat that justifies high costs, since each option carries serious risks and uncertain odds.
recommendations: Reserve high-risk escalation for a threat judged existential; otherwise seek terms that stop Iranian attacks on shipping.
Avoid sanctioning Chinese firms over Iran trade given the risk of a global financial shock and Chinese retaliation on critical minerals.
Account for Gulf energy infrastructure exposure before renewing strikes.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for Hudson Institute, argue that the Biden administration lost moral and strategic clarity on Gaza after October 7. They contend that political pressure, biased media coverage and activist demands shaped deliberations and messaging, which prolonged the war and fed antisemitism. They defend Israel's right to fight Hamas, say Israeli conduct deserves scrutiny but has been judged by a double standard, and reject the genocide label. They fault Washington for not challenging Hamas-run casualty figures, for not planning a postwar exit, and for not stressing Hamas's use of civilian sites. They conclude that Democrats must affirm Israel's cause, support scrutiny of its conduct, and oppose selective condemnation if they want to govern again.
brief.argument: The authors argue that the Biden administration lost moral and strategic clarity on Gaza, and that Democrats must affirm Israel's war against Hamas while accepting scrutiny of its conduct.

Challenge Hamas-run casualty figures and reject the genocide characterisation.
Publicly stress Hamas's use of civilian infrastructure and its diversion of aid.
Set out an explicit postwar plan for Gaza instead of a political vacuum.

items.title: Will Europe’s Protests Mark a Turning Point?
items.summary: CFR President Michael Froman analyzes the recent European protests ahead of upcoming elections and changing U.S. relations.

ai.sum: CFR President Michael Froman analyses recent European protests ahead of upcoming elections and shifting US-European relations.

brief.summary: Michael Froman, CFR President, argues that recent French protests reflect a fundamental collapse of the French social contract rather than ordinary street mobilisation. He points to weak investment in education, a pension burden carried by a shrinking workforce, anaemic growth, and youth unemployment of about one in five. He links this to a possible debt crisis, rising borrowing costs, and an ascendant far right heading into France's 2027 election. He also argues that an abrupt shift in US policy toward Russia, including waiving new sanctions and praising Putin, leaves Europe still dependent on Washington for influence over Ukraine, since European rearmament will take years. He concludes that Europe must fix its structural weaknesses, or face a long winter.
brief.argument: Europe's protests signal a deeper collapse of the social contract that, combined with fiscal strain and US unreliability on Ukraine, forces European states to reform or remain geopolitically dependent.
recommendations: Implement economic reforms along the lines of the Draghi and Letta reports
Consolidate Europe's military industrial base
Operate more effectively together with a degree of strategic autonomy
Address political dysfunction in Western democracies

items.title: North Korea may be the biggest winner of Russia’s war in Ukraine
items.summary: Pyongyang is gaining combat experience, technology, and money by supporting Russia's invasion, raising security risks for the Indo-Pacific. The post North Korea may be the biggest winner of Russia’s war in Ukraine appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues North Korea gains combat experience, technology and money from supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.

brief.summary: The authors argue that North Korea may be one of the largest beneficiaries of Russia's war in Ukraine despite not being a formal belligerent. They say Pyongyang gains combat experience from deploying troops since October 2024, battlefield testing and improvement of its weapons, large financial returns from arms exports and sanctions evasion, and technology transfers from Russia that may help close gaps in space, precision-strike, drone and naval nuclear propulsion capabilities. Against this, Russia and Ukraine bear heavy casualties and economic costs. The authors contend the partnership weakens arms-transfer sanctions enforcement and could embolden Kim Jong Un, raising miscalculation risk on the Korean peninsula and in the wider Indo-Pacific. They end by raising open questions about China's stance, the durability of the Russia partnership after the war, and implications for US planning and nuclear deterrence.
brief.argument: North Korea's support for Russia has yielded substantial military, financial and technological gains that could reshape the security balance in the Indo-Pacific.

items.title: Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev Warns President John F. Kennedy of “Catastrophic Consequences”—Cuban Missile Crisis, Day Eight
items.summary: U.S. success in rallying support in the Americas for a naval quarantine of Cuba and a strong speech by the U.S. ambassador to the United Nation is eclipsed by an unyielding response from Moscow.

ai.sum: This historical CFR piece recounts Khrushchev warning Kennedy of catastrophic consequences during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.

brief.summary: The authors, writing as a CFR retrospective on Day Eight of the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, narrate how the crisis went public and how the U.S. built a legal and diplomatic case for a naval quarantine. They describe the Organization of American States vote backing the quarantine, Adlai Stevenson's forceful Security Council speech, and the ExComm's daily deliberations, including reconnaissance flights and the discovery of vulnerable aircraft on both sides. The piece contrasts this with Khrushchev's unyielding letter, which accused Washington of lawlessness and warned of catastrophic consequences. It closes with Kennedy's blunt reply demanding Soviet compliance and Robert Kennedy's secret meeting with Ambassador Dobrynin, which revealed that Dobrynin was unaware of the missiles. The author presents the day as the start of the most dangerous phase of the crisis.
brief.argument: The U.S. won international legal and diplomatic backing for the quarantine, but Khrushchev's defiant reply made the crisis's most dangerous days begin.

ai.sum: Eastern Libya's parliament ratified the 2019 maritime boundary deal with Türkiye, drawing objections from Egypt, Greece and Israel over Eastern Mediterranean claims.

brief.summary: The authors argue that eastern Libya's parliament ratifying the 2019 maritime delimitation memorandum with Türkiye is a major geopolitical win for Ankara, expanding its influence in the Eastern Mediterranean. They frame the vote as a sign of the political ambitions of Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the Libyan National Army, who has been cultivating ties with Greece, Türkiye, Israel, the United States and Egypt. The piece stresses that the deal matters because defining exclusive economic zones determines control over gas-rich seabed resources. It describes a reversal, since the Haftars were once at odds with Ankara, and notes that the ratified zone overlaps Egypt's EEZ, prompting Cairo's swift rejection. The authors present Egypt's position as rooted both in Cairo-Ankara rivalry and in concrete problems for its eastern Mediterranean energy plans.
brief.argument: Eastern Libya's ratification of the Türkiye maritime deal is a hard-won Turkish geopolitical victory that reshuffles regional alliances and creates new challenges for Egypt.
brief.turkey: The ratification gives Ankara a legal and maritime foothold in the Eastern Mediterranean, but it also sharpens its rivalry with Egypt over overlapping EEZs.

Iran retains know-how, enriched material and some centrifuge capacity, and IAEA verification has largely collapsed. They describe Tehran shifting from calculated latency to calculated ambiguity: the religious fatwa against nuclear weapons, long the doctrinal anchor, has been eroded in public debate, with parliamentarians and security officials openly backing an 'active nuclear deterrence' and even NPT withdrawal. brief.argument: Iran's nuclear doctrine has moved from latency to deliberate ambiguity, so proliferation risk remains high despite military strikes and the diplomatic track is weak.

Work to restore IAEA verification access and insight into Iran's programme
Address the Hormuz dispute as a precondition or parallel element of nuclear talks

ai.sum: An article traces the Palestinian flag's role in French student and social protests since late September.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Palestinian flag has become a versatile political symbol in France, carried by students, trade unionists, the left, the far right and even looters during the autumn 2026 protest wave. Tracing its rise from campus protests in spring 2024 to the National Assembly, they show how different actors use it for divergent purposes, from solidarity and mobilisation to demonising protest as a security or identity threat. Palestinians themselves, they contend, have little control over what the flag signifies or who holds it. The flag has travelled abroad while Palestinians themselves remain largely excluded from the same spaces, so their own national story recedes behind other people's narratives. The piece is a reflective commentary rather than a policy paper.
brief.argument: The Palestinian flag has been detached from Palestinians and turned into a contested symbol that different French groups use for opposing aims, while Palestinians lose control of its meaning.

items.title: Pete Hegseth’s Campaign to Remake the U.S. Military
items.summary: The secretary of defense’s shake-up of the senior ranks raises hard questions about the future of U.S. military leadership. Carla Anne Robbins turns to the New York Times’ Greg Jaffe to explain who is being pushed out, and why it matters.

ai.sum: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is reshaping senior US military ranks, pushing out officers and raising questions about leadership.

brief.summary: The authors, Carla Anne Robbins in conversation with the New York Times' Greg Jaffe, examine Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's effort to reshape senior U.S. military leadership. They report that he has fired or blocked promotions of more than eighty generals and admirals, with almost half being women or minority officers. They attribute his drive partly to grievances over Iraq and Afghanistan and to a worldview they describe as Christian nationalist and culture-war driven. The piece argues the most visible effect is on the senior ranks, with women hit hardest, while the ousted leaders have stayed publicly silent. Jaffe is less optimistic that current chiefs, such as Gen. Dan Caine, will speak frankly to civilian leaders. The authors identify Congress, where lawmakers of both parties resist Hegseth's nominations and budget requests, as his main obstacle.
brief.argument: Hegseth's purge of senior officers is reshaping U.S. military leadership along ideological lines, with lasting costs to advice quality and institutional talent, and Congress is the main check on it.

items.title: What the new arrest warrant for Raúl Castro means for Cuba’s future
items.summary: Washington’s latest pressure on the Cuban regime comes as Cuba’s economic and humanitarian crisis spirals from bad to worse. The post What the new arrest warrant for Raúl Castro means for Cuba’s future appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Washington issued a new arrest warrant for Raúl Castro amid Cuba's worsening economic and humanitarian crisis.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a new arrest warrant for Raúl Castro, tied to the 1996 shoot-down of two Brothers to the Rescue aircraft, signals US seriousness about accountability, even though it will not soon bring him into custody. They describe Cuba's economic and humanitarian collapse as worsened by lost trade, the drying up of Venezuelan oil after Maduro's removal, and US sanctions. They contend that the regime prioritises keeping power over the welfare of Cubans, that its economic reforms are a charade, and that only a complete political transition, including dismantling the security structure and establishing democracy, can serve both US security goals and Cuban welfare. They say early planning for post-transition reconstruction with international financial institutions and the exile community should begin now, and that Cuban opposition groups grouped under the Freedom Accord should have a seat in any serious negotiation.
brief.argument: Lasting change in Cuba requires a complete political transition that dismantles the regime's security structure, with Washington's pressure and accountability measures supporting it.
recommendations: Continue direct messaging to the Cuban people about a post-regime economic model
Systematically sanction current Cuban leaders and pursue legal accountability
Begin early planning and initial funding commitments with international financial institutions and partners for post-transition reconstruction
Give Cuban pro-democracy groups, including the Freedom Accord coalition, a place in any serious negotiation

items.title: Israel’s Election: Who’s Who and What’s at Stake?
items.summary: Israel’s October 27 election could reshape the country’s political landscape, but neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition has a clear path to a governing majority. The outcome of the vote could determine not only who leads Israel, but how the country contends with various domestic and foreign policy concerns.

ai.sum: Israel's October 27 election may not produce a clear governing majority for Netanyahu's allies or the opposition.

brief.summary: The CFR piece, drawing on experts Elliott Abrams and Steven A. Cook, frames Israel's October 27 election as possibly among the most consequential in the country's history. The authors explain Israel's proportional system, the 3.25 percent threshold and the 61-seat majority requirement, and map the two blocs: the Netanyahu coalition and an anti-Netanyahu 'change bloc' that has not agreed on a successor. They argue neither side has a clear path to 61 seats, so a government may depend on concessions such as a rotational premiership, sitting with Arab parties, or sitting with ultra-Orthodox parties, and that prolonged negotiations or a further election are plausible. On foreign policy, the authors expect little abrupt change; a new government would mainly alter tone, possibly toward settler violence in the West Bank and relations with Jordan.
brief.argument: Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition has a clear route to a 61-seat majority, so coalition arithmetic will force hard concessions and may produce a further election, while foreign policy would change mainly in tone rather than substance.

items.summary: A new Israeli government could offer a chance to reset strained relations with Washington. The post The US-Israel relationship needs a reset. Here’s how to do it. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues a new Israeli government could offer a chance to reset strained US-Israel relations.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US-Israel alliance is at once at a high point operationally and eroding politically, and that it needs a deliberate reset. They point to joint operations against Iran and the hostage deal as proof of strength, but cite Israeli government decisions (freezing Gaza 'day after' planning, West Bank violence, partisan alignment), US Congressional votes and falling public support as sources of strain. Their remedy is a seven-pillar roadmap: shared democratic values and bipartisanship, a diplomatic initiative on Gaza, the Palestinians, Lebanon, Syria and Saudi normalisation, a transition from aid to partnership in the next MOU from 2029, Israel as a regional air-defence hub, a deeper defence-industrial partnership, cooperation on AI and space, and a institutionalised Strategic Dialogue run by professionals. The piece is written by a former head of Israel's Defense Ministry Political-Military Bureau.
brief.argument: The US-Israel alliance is operationally stronger than ever but politically fraying, so it needs a structured reset that shifts it from aid to partnership while restoring institutional anchors.
recommendations: Implement the current 2019-2028 MOU in full and phase the shift from aid to partnership in the next MOU from 2029, offset by joint R&D and co-production
Lead a structured Israeli diplomatic initiative on Gaza demilitarisation, a Palestinian political horizon designed with Washington, and an end to West Bank extremist violence
Modernise export-control arrangements and advance the defence-industrial working group and FUTURES Act cooperation
Create a multi-year Strategic Dialogue co-chaired by the US national security advisor and the head of Israel's National Security Council, staffed by career professionals

items.title: An Emboldened Iran Could Trigger an IS Comeback

ai.sum: Washington Institute analysis argues an emboldened Iran could trigger a resurgence of the Islamic State.

brief.summary: The authors argue that IS has been largely defeated in Iraq and Syria, with attacks down sharply, but the conditions that produced it, including Sunni Arab rejection of Iranian and proxy control and some support for violent fundamentalism, remain latent. The main trigger they identify is a new round of Iranian expansion following a US withdrawal without a security alternative. They note that neither Arab states, Europe, Türkiye nor Israel could easily replace the US in containing Iran, since leadership and convening power rest with Washington. They conclude that if the US and Israel fail in their war on Iran, Tehran's regional dominance could revive a Sunni extremist counterweight, though an IS comeback is currently unlikely and renewed US engagement cannot be assumed.
brief.argument: If the Iran war ends inconclusively and Iranian regional expansion goes unchecked, the conditions for an IS revival in Iraq and Syria could return.
recommendations: Maintain the US and anti-IS coalition's counter-IS capabilities, including OIR's authority to strike high-value targets in Syria
Sustain military assistance and training to Baghdad
Ensure a credible regional security architecture is in place to contain Iran if the US steps back
brief.turkey: Türkiye has a long history of containing Iran only within its immediate near abroad, so it is unlikely to fill a wider containment role if the US withdraws, which bears on Syria and Iraq security planning.

ai.sum: Hudson Institute commentary examines whether an America First position on Israel can be effective.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a genuine America First position on Israel treats the alliance as a strategic asset: Israel is a force multiplier against Iran, and Iran's links to China, Russia and North Korea bear on containing China. They say antisemitic conspiracy claims, promoted by Tucker Carlson and Nick Fuentes, corrode American cohesion and allied relations, and that the right's leaders, notably JD Vance, Kevin Roberts and Yoram Hazony, hedge toward these figures to keep political access. They also contend national conservatism's Principle Four, privileging Christianity while only protecting minorities, sits uneasily with the founding's equal citizenship, as Washington's 1790 Newport letter shows. The piece concludes that the defence of allies and of equal citizenship are linked.
brief.argument: A coherent America First policy on Israel must treat the alliance as strategic power, and defeating the antisemitic conspiracism that undermines it requires the constitutional principle of equal citizenship.
recommendations: Frame the Israel partnership in terms of American interests and Eurasian containment rather than religious identity.
Break political association with figures who promote antisemitic conspiracy theories, rather than distancing only from their crudest expressions.

But today Taiz has found itself in the news again,…

ai.sum: Al Majalla profiles Taiz, Yemen, describing its resistance to Houthi attacks since 2014 and its cultural role.

brief.summary: The authors present Taiz as a historic centre of civic life, learning and religious coexistence in Yemen. They trace its role from the Rasulid era, when it was the political capital of Shafi'i Islam and home to major schools and libraries, through its merchant families and modern political awakening after the 1962 and 1963 revolutions. They describe the city's sectarian tolerance, its Sufi traditions centred on Yafrus, and the demographic split between Shafi'i communities in the south and west and Zaydi communities in the north. The piece frames this heritage against the current Houthi offensive and siege of the city, which the authors present as a continuation of attacks that began after 2014. The argument is largely historical and cultural rather than a policy paper.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Taiz has long been a centre of enlightenment, commerce and religious coexistence, and that this heritage makes it a target for the Houthis.

items.title: Technology , War , and the Limits of Innovation Power in the Middle East

ai.sum: A Washington Institute analysis examines the limits of technology-driven innovation power in the Middle East.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Israel and Iran have each used technological and tactical innovation to achieve results in the 2025 and 2026 wars, but that these gains do not translate into durable strategic outcomes. Israel's model rests on bespoke, intelligence-heavy operations (the pager attacks, targeted strikes, AI-assisted targeting) that are effective in short campaigns but hard to repeat once adversaries adapt. Iran's model relies on cheap, expendable and scalable systems such as Shahed drones, fibre-optic FPV drones used by Hezbollah, and AI-generated propaganda, which impose costs through attrition and asymmetry. The authors contend that the impasse persists mainly for political reasons: Israel has not defined an end state for Gaza, Lebanon or Iran, Iran's IRGC benefits economically from confrontation, and the US lacks durable domestic consensus. Technology alone, they conclude, cannot produce a settlement.
brief.argument: Innovation power yields tactical successes for both Israel and Iran, but without political conditions for a settlement these gains cannot become durable strategic outcomes.
recommendations: Define a durable security architecture for Gaza, including a role for a reformed Palestinian Authority and Arab partners
Pursue a political settlement with Lebanon and a disarmament pathway for Hezbollah
Build an Iran policy designed to outlast a single election cycle
Consolidate military gains through diplomacy, policy and digital public diplomacy, including counters to cheap AI-enabled propaganda
brief.turkey: The piece implies that Türkiye faces a regional environment where cheap drones and AI propaganda lower the cost of coercion, and where Gulf deescalation with Tehran and the Saudi normalisation question shape the broader diplomatic field.

items.title: Ukrainians are not fighting for Zelenskyy. They are fighting for national survival.
items.summary: Trump and Putin both seem to think that removing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would set the stage for a Kremlin-friendly peace deal, but most Ukrainians see the war as a fight for national survival that does not depend on any one man, writes Peter Dickinson. The post Ukrainians are not fighting for Zelenskyy. They are fighting for national survival. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues most Ukrainians see the war as national survival rather than loyalty to Zelenskyy.

brief.summary: The author argues that Trump and Putin both wrongly treat Zelenskyy as the main obstacle to peace. He notes that Zelenskyy has accepted every US-backed ceasefire proposal and offered major territorial concessions, while Moscow rejected them. The piece holds that Ukrainians are fighting for national survival rather than for Zelenskyy personally, and that most would resist any replacement pursuing a peace on Russian terms. It describes Putin's rhetoric denying Ukrainian nationhood and the mass detentions and russification in occupied areas as evidence that Ukrainians see the war as existential. The conclusion is that removing Zelenskyy would not change the trajectory of the war, because the resistance rests on collective will rather than one leader.
brief.argument: Ukraine's resistance is driven by an existential fear of Russian annihilation, so replacing Zelenskyy would not produce a Russia-friendly peace.

items.title: Brazil’s Runoff Election Is a Close Race Between Lula and Bolsonaro
items.summary: This week on The Spillover, Rebecca Patterson and Shannon O’Neil, senior vice president of studies at CFR, discuss Brazil’s October 25 presidential runoff and whether either leader can deliver what both voters and markets want. Brazil’s runoff presidential election is on October 25. Patterson notes that incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, […]

ai.sum: CFR discussion previews Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro and its market implications.

brief.summary: The authors, CFR's Rebecca Patterson and Shannon O'Neil, argue that Brazil's October 2026 presidential runoff is close, with markets favouring Flávio Bolsonaro because they expect him to rein in a precarious fiscal position, while voters are focused on cost of living, household debt and crime. They contend that fiscal consolidation will be hard under either candidate: much spending is locked into Brazil's long constitution, centrist parties in Congress trade votes for spending, and any reform window is short and likely to be eroded by politics. Patterson notes that past Brazilian first-round leaders usually win the runoff. O'Neil stresses that Flávio's campaign has focused on amnesty for his jailed father and the Supreme Court more than on fiscal reform. The piece also widens to Argentina, where Milei's austerity has brought inflation down but left household debt high, and uses the episode to draw lessons for developed economies facing similar debt dynamics.
brief.argument: Brazil's runoff is a near tie in which markets are pricing a fiscal turn that the structure of Brazilian politics makes hard to deliver under either candidate.

items.title: The Iran War and the Midterms
items.summary: We Discuss: Mentioned on the Episode: Cole Bucy and Nate Swanson, “Trump Unleashed,” Foreign Policy

ai.sum: CFR podcast episode discusses the Iran war and its implications for the US midterm elections.

brief.summary: The authors, Cole Bucy and Nate Swanson, discuss a strategic stalemate between the United States and Iran after months of war. They argue that Washington has limited options: escalate militarily, pursue a diplomatic off-ramp (the June memorandum collapsed), or continue a costly contest of economic endurance over the Strait of Hormuz. They judge that Iran's regime is hurting economically but shows no elite or security defections and will fight on. Bucy argues that President Trump, constrained by oil prices and unpopularity of the war before the midterms, may see a window for escalation afterward, possibly including renewed strikes, decapitation attempts or a symbolic 'season finale' strike on Pickaxe Mountain to paper over the lack of a clear win. Swanson is skeptical that Iran's calculations are driven by the midterms and sees no good options for either side. The conversation is a CFR podcast, and the authors frame their views as speculation in a private capacity.
brief.argument: The US is stuck in a strategic stalemate with Iran, and after the midterms Trump may escalate militarily, though the authors doubt escalation will produce a clean victory.

items.title: Why Kazakhstan Joined Both the American and Chinese AI Initiatives
items.summary: Kazakhstan did not choose between Washington’s Pax Silica and Beijing’s WAICO: it joined both. It needs technology from both superpowers, and a say in the rules.

ai.sum: Kazakhstan joined both the US-led Pax Silica and China's WAICO AI initiatives to access technology from both and shape rules.

brief.summary: The author argues that Kazakhstan joined both the US-led Pax Silica initiative and China-led WAICO because it needs technology from both superpowers and a voice in the rules, rather than choosing sides. Pragmatism drives this: the US and China hold the leading AI capabilities, while Kazakhstan offers leverage through uranium and critical minerals such as tungsten. Its AI push, framed as both a state-efficiency tool and an export industry, relies on American chips and data centres, Chinese connectivity and models, Russian internet routes and nuclear power, and UAE partnerships, with European influence in its legal framework. The author also contends that neither initiative provides the testing and governance capacity needed, since that ability sits mainly inside frontier AI firms. Tokayev's proposals for common standards and an expert platform are described as capabilities that exist nowhere yet, making binding rules increasingly important for smaller states.
brief.argument: Kazakhstan joins both US and Chinese AI initiatives because it needs their technology and wants a say in the rules, and neither initiative yet supplies the governance capacity it requires.
recommendations: Establish common standards for testing and certifying AI systems
Create a permanent expert platform on AI regulation and ethics
Ensure WAICO and Pax Silica develop rules that constrain the strong, not only bilateral bargains

items.title: Trump's Putin Overtures Deserve Criticism. But Outrage Won't End the Ukraine War.
items.summary: As Trump’s envoy meets Putin in St. Petersburg, critics accuse the White House of abandoning Ukraine. CFR’s Thomas Graham argues that this criticism may be warranted, but dialogue and diplomacy remain the only route to a settlement that preserves Ukraine’s sovereignty and alignment with the West.

ai.sum: As Trump's envoy meets Putin in St. Petersburg, CFR analysis argues dialogue is the only route to a settlement preserving Ukraine's sovereignty.

brief.summary: The authors argue that criticism of Trump's overtures to Putin may be justified, but outrage does little to clarify the hard choices facing the West and Ukraine. They contend a just peace is unattainable: Russia will keep most seized land and Putin will not face trial, so the realistic aim is an imperfect peace that preserves Ukrainian sovereignty and keeps open Ukraine's path toward European security integration. This requires continued Western weapons and intelligence support, with sanctions judged to have diminishing returns. Dialogue is necessary, and the author sees normalization not as a return to post-Cold War cooperation but as the kind of managed, rivalrous relations that prevailed during the Cold War, with reliable channels to avert crises. Over time, Europe will need deterrence along the frontier, followed by arms control and renewed commercial and societal ties, since Russia and Europe share a continent.
brief.argument: Outrage at Trump's Putin overtures is understandable, but the West should pursue an achievable, imperfect peace that preserves Ukraine's sovereignty and European path, paired with managed dialogue and eventual Cold War-style normalization with Russia.
recommendations: Maintain strong Western military aid and intelligence support to Ukraine to halt or reverse Russian battlefield gains and blunt aerial bombardment
Measure Witkoff's talks against what is achievable rather than against an idealised just peace
Pursue slow integration of Ukraine into European security structures short of NATO membership
Establish reliable channels of communication with Russia and later arms control agreements to prevent escalation

items.title: The new Middle East is modular
items.summary: In the Middle East today, states are aligning issue by issue, not choosing sides. They cooperate in one area and compete in the next. This modular alignment is shaping the region, even as it manages the shocks of war and energy-market volatility. The post The new Middle East is modular appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues Middle Eastern states now align issue by issue rather than in fixed blocs.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Middle East is not splitting into two blocs but is instead moving toward modular alignment, where states cooperate with the same partners in some sectors while rivaling them in others. They examine the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan-Egypt grouping (the R4) and the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, finding deep bilateral frictions over Libya, Syria, the Eastern Mediterranean and Lebanon. They contend that the UAE-Israel relationship is also case-by-case rather than a bloc, and that economic fragility and divergent priorities undermine binding commitments. The Mecca pact, they say, is far weaker than NATO's Article 5 in practice, and Gulf states increasingly act on their own strategic autonomy, even as they do not break with Washington.
brief.argument: The Middle East is realigning through issue-specific, modular partnerships rather than binding regional blocs, because rivalries and economic constraints prevent members from subordinating their interests.
recommendations: Western capitals should not expect Gulf states to finance regional reconstruction altruistically, since Gulf leaders now invest only where it makes financial sense.
Analysts should judge regional alignments sector by sector rather than as bloc membership.
Mecca Agreement members should build joint infrastructure and binding commitments if they want the pact to function like NATO's Article 5.
brief.turkey: Türkiye's R4 and Mecca Agreement commitments are shallow, and its frictions with Egypt over Libya and gas, and with Saudi Arabia over Syria, mean it should expect cooperation on defence industry and trade rather than a binding alliance.

items.title: Surging Export Similarity is Fueling Advanced Economy Trade Tensions with China
items.summary: Growing global imbalances are only one source of trade frictions with China. Another is the soaring similarity in the export baskets of China and the advanced-economy countries.

ai.sum: CFR analysis argues rising similarity in China's and advanced economies' export baskets is fuelling trade tensions.

brief.summary: The authors argue that trade friction with China is driven not only by aggregate global imbalances but by a rising overlap between China's export basket and that of advanced economies. Advanced economies shifted away from basic manufactures after the first China shock, but since 2016 (chemicals) and 2023 (machinery) the similarity index has climbed steeply, with electric vehicles the largest single driver, lifting Japan and Germany by roughly ten points since 2007. They contend unilateral tariffs are flawed because duties get circumvented, as with plug-in hybrids after the EU's 2024 EV duties, and because overcapacity is merely diverted to third markets. They see the October 7 excess-capacity statement by fifteen economies as a possible path, provided it has agreed triggers, coordinated responses, a credible exit for China verified by members' own monitoring, and an end to threats against partners.
brief.argument: Rising export similarity between China and advanced economies, led by EVs and machinery, makes unilateral tariffs ineffective and requires a coordinated multilateral response to Chinese overcapacity.
recommendations: Adopt a multilateral excess-capacity framework with agreed triggers and coordinated responses to diversion.
Give China a verifiable exit by lifting measures as subsidies are demonstrably cut, judged by members' own monitoring rather than Beijing's reporting.
Stop threatening overcapacity action against partners Washington is courting.
brief.turkey: Türkiye sits outside the advanced-economy core but is exposed to the same diversion of Chinese overcapacity into third markets, so any coordinated trade-defence regime will shape its export access and tariff exposure.

items.summary: The government secured the withdrawal of foreign partners before securing obedience from armed factions. That leaves Baghdad with less leverage against Iran’s allies in Iraq. ai.sum: Analysis argues Iraq's government secured the US-led coalition's withdrawal before disarming armed factions, weakening its leverage against Iran-aligned groups.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the withdrawal of the US-led coalition from Iraq was a genuine act of Iraqi sovereignty, but that it has left Baghdad with less leverage over Iran-aligned armed factions. They describe how groups such as Kataib Hezbollah and Asaib Ahl al-Haq hold formal positions within the Popular Mobilization Forces, keep ties to the IRGC Quds Force, and sustain political and commercial networks that resist government orders. The piece points to Kaabi's flag-trampling video, the postponed weapons-control deadline, and disputes over Iranian flights as evidence of this challenge to Prime Minister Zaidi's authority. The authors contend that the coalition had supplied an alternative to factional security ties, and that its removal raises the stakes of Iraq's dependence on Iranian gas. They call for enforceable disarmament, verified personnel lists, audits of militia-linked contracts, and external support that strengthens state institutions rather than punishing the population.
brief.argument: Iraq's sovereignty over its security will remain incomplete until Baghdad can enforce its decisions against Iran-aligned armed factions that are embedded in state institutions, now that the US-led coalition has departed.
recommendations: Bring heavy weapons into state arsenals under independent inspection to verify disarmament
Tie public salaries to verified personnel lists and obedience to lawful orders
Audit militia-linked contracts and restore state control over border revenues
Diversify energy and electricity links, including with Gulf states, and protect those projects from political interference

Experiences differ sharply: the UAE absorbed far more Iranian strikes than Qatar, reinforcing Abu Dhabi's preference for a decisive outcome and Doha's and Muscat's preference for mediation. The piece holds that Washington keeps expecting the GCC to act as one bloc, treating disagreement as institutional failure rather than geopolitical reality. Using the EU as a model, it urges the US to engage the GCC where interests align and bilaterally where they diverge. It highlights Kuwait, which avoided unilateral moves despite heavy attacks, and the Mecca Agreement among Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, which excludes the UAE.
brief.argument: The Gulf states are diverging on Iran, defence and diplomacy, so Washington should stop treating the GCC as a single strategic actor.
recommendations: Give the GCC the same room for internal disagreement that the EU receives, working through the council where interests align and bilaterally where they do not.
Shorten the path from request to delivery for air and missile defence and counter-drone systems.
Approach co-development with Gulf partners as a strategic investment rather than a concession.
Consult GCC partners early and collectively on any arrangement with Tehran, including missiles, drones and proxies.

The author recounts how the ExComm debated the wording of the speech, settling on 'quarantine' rather than 'blockade' on Rusk's advice, and narrowing the quarantine to offensive equipment. It also covers the contingency invasion plans, which Kennedy found too slow, and the letters sent to 43 world leaders. The essay ends by noting that the public knew nothing of these deliberations.
brief.argument: Kennedy's choice of 'quarantine' and his narrow initial scope were deliberate diplomatic and political decisions meant to signal resolve while limiting provocation.

Valentina Sader argues that either winner must manage US-China competition, Mercosur and Argentina, and a more right-leaning Congress, with Lula favouring diversification and Bolsonaro closer alignment with Washington.
brief.argument: Brazil's October runoff will shape its trade, security, fiscal and regional alignment, but the constraints of fiscal credibility, US-China balance and a more right-leaning Congress limit how far either candidate can shift course.
recommendations: Washington should conclude the critical minerals agreement with Brazil and expand DFC and EXIM financing.
Brazil's next government should establish a durable fiscal anchor to lower interest-rate risk premiums.
Brazil should keep pragmatic trade ties with both the United States and China regardless of the winner.

They argue the speech under-described the role of algorithms in building radicalising echo chambers, undersold the vulnerability of young people to online radicalisation, and omitted hate crime, which rose in England and Wales. They conclude that responses must be bespoke, locally rooted and properly resourced, that governments should support parents and communities, and that soft power and social cohesion are linked to national vulnerability.
brief.argument: MI5's threat update was right to frame security as a whole-of-society matter, but it underplayed how algorithm-driven echo chambers and youth radicalisation drive extremism.
recommendations: Build governmental resilience models tailored to different age groups, especially children and adolescents.

items.title: Establishing Battery Supply Chain Resilience for Drones
items.summary: Militaries have spent more than a century operating with fuel and ammunition as limits of combat endurance. They are only beginning to treat batteries with the same operational seriousness, as small unmanned systems move from niche equipment to mass-consumption weapons. ai.sum: War on the Rocks article argues militaries must treat drone batteries as a supply-chain vulnerability and calls for diversification.

brief.summary: The authors argue that military drone batteries have become a central constraint on combat endurance, as small unmanned systems move toward mass consumption. They say defence is a price taker in a commercial battery market dwarfed by electric vehicles and grid storage, so it cannot build a purely military ecosystem. Their proposed three-part resilience approach combines a strategic battery reserve, domestic and allied manufacturing with competitive suppliers, and research into new chemistries. They also stress that domestic assembly does not equal supply-chain independence, since Chinese inputs persist deeper in the chain. Tactical charging and power logistics are treated as part of the problem, and the piece urges matching each dependency to consequence and recovery time when choosing between commercial scale, pre-qualified sources, protected capacity, or inventory.
brief.argument: Drone batteries are now a combat-endurance and industrial vulnerability that defence must manage by matching each dependency's consequence and recovery time to the right mix of commercial scale, allied sourcing, protected capacity and strategic reserves.
recommendations: Establish a strategic battery reserve sized to bridge supply interruptions until qualified production is restored.
Standardise battery form factors and interfaces, aggregate military demand, and qualify multiple commercial and allied suppliers.
Protect capacity for high-consequence, slow-recovery dependencies through long-term contracts, capacity reservations or sovereign production.
Fund long-term battery research and government innovation programmes to develop chemistries that reduce exposure to concentrated materials.
brief.turkey: For Türkiye's drone-heavy force planning and defence industry, the piece points to the need to trace battery sub-tier dependencies and to plan for charging and power logistics alongside fuel and munitions.

brief.argument: Europe's resilience to Russian hybrid warfare requires a funded, locally delivered social cohesion pillar, because disinformation alone cannot correct the grievances that hybrid campaigns exploit.

items.title: Guns, Growth, and the German Reinvention of Military Keynesianism
items.summary: In March 2025, Germany did more than loosen a fiscal rule. It fused two national emergencies — a deteriorating European security order and a deteriorating industrial model — into a single constitutional bargain. The reform de facto exempted German defense expenditure from any domestic budgetary ceiling — as the German Bundesbank itself has acknowledged — and enabled a military expansion of extraordinary proportions. E.U. debt rules of 3 percent of GDP for annual government…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Germany's March 2025 constitutional change, which effectively exempted defence spending from the debt brake, was a logroll: security conservatives, Social Democrats and Greens each traded support for their priorities, with the spending justified in shared security and modernisation terms. They link it to 'China Shock 2.0', as Chinese overcapacity hits German industry, and note that defence procurement overlaps with the capabilities that sector needs. Drawing on the American rearmament of 1950-53, they say military Keynesianism works best when the spending absorbs slack, goes to a net arms exporter, and drives frontier technology. Germany meets some preconditions but its procurement is still weighted to conventional platforms, with frontier-tech shares falling. Procurement rules such as the 25 million euro Bundestag approval threshold and a risk-averse culture block innovation. They conclude Germany has a coalition but not yet a growth strategy.
brief.argument: Germany's defence buildup has become a politically durable military-Keynesian logroll, but without a deliberate innovation-focused procurement strategy it will cushion industrial decline rather than restore growth.
recommendations: Link military procurement explicitly to an industrial strategy aimed at innovation and productivity
Raise the 25 million euro Bundestag approval threshold or otherwise ease approval for innovative contracts
